sections.heading: What is the Sorting & Custom Comparators Pattern?
sections.content: Many problems become easy once the data is in the right order. Sorting costs O(n log n) and often turns a hard O(n²) search into a simple scan, two pointers pass or greedy choice. When the natural order is not what you need (sort by length, by frequency, by end time, or by a custom rule), you define a comparator that tells the sort how two elements compare.

sections.heading: When to Use It
items: Sorting makes the problem simpler: duplicates, pairs, intervals, greedy choices
You need elements ordered by a custom rule (length, frequency, multiple keys)
The problem says 'arrange to form the largest number' or 'sort by ...'
You can afford O(n log n) time
Values are in a small range, so counting or bucket sort gives O(n)
You need the order of objects, pairs, arrays or strings, not only numbers

sections.heading: What Kotlin Uses Internally
sections.content: On the JVM, sorting primitive arrays like IntArray uses a dual-pivot quicksort (average O(n log n), worst case rarely seen). Sorting objects, lists and Array<T> uses TimSort, which is stable and O(n log n). Stable means equal elements keep their original relative order, which matters when you sort by one key and then another.

sections.heading: Basic Sorting in Kotlin
sections.code:
val nums = intArrayOf(5, 2, 9, 1)
nums.sort()                           // in place, ascending
nums.sortDescending()                 // in place, descending
val asc = nums.sortedArray()          // new IntArray
val list = listOf(5, 2, 9, 1)
val sortedList = list.sorted()        // new List, ascending
val desc = list.sortedDescending()    // new List, descending

val mutable = mutableListOf(5, 2, 9, 1)
mutable.sort()                        // in place for MutableList

// Sort only a range [from, to)
nums.sort(1, 3)

sections.heading: Sorting With Comparators
sections.code:
val words = listOf("banana", "fig", "apple", "kiwi")

words.sortedBy { it.length }                       // by one key
words.sortedByDescending { it.length }
words.sortedWith(compareBy({ it.length }, { it }))   // length, then alphabetical
words.sortedWith(compareByDescending<String> { it.length }.thenBy { it })

// Explicit comparator
words.sortedWith(Comparator { a, b -> a.length - b.length })
words.sortedWith { a, b -> b.length.compareTo(a.length) }   // descending by length

// In place on a mutable list or array
val arr = arrayOf("banana", "fig", "apple")
arr.sortWith(compareBy { it.length })

sections.heading: Safe Comparator Rules
Sorting 2D Arrays and Pairs
sections.code:
val intervals = arrayOf(intArrayOf(5, 8), intArrayOf(1, 3), intArrayOf(1, 2))

intervals.sortBy { it[0] }                                  // by start
intervals.sortWith(compareBy({ it[0] }, { it[1] }))         // start, then end
intervals.sortWith(compareBy({ it[0] }, { -it[1] }))        // start asc, end desc

val pairs = listOf(Pair(1, "b"), Pair(1, "a"), Pair(0, "z"))
pairs.sortedWith(compareBy({ it.first }, { it.second }))

// Sort indices by value (keep the original array)
val values = intArrayOf(30, 10, 20)
val order = values.indices.sortedBy { values[it] }          // [1, 2, 0]

sections.code:
fun mergeSort(a: IntArray, l: Int = 0, r: Int = a.size - 1) {
    if (l >= r) return
    val m = l + (r - l) / 2
    mergeSort(a, l, m)
    mergeSort(a, m + 1, r)
    val temp = IntArray(r - l + 1)
    var i = l
    var j = m + 1
    var k = 0
    while (i <= m && j <= r) temp[k++] = if (a[i] <= a[j]) a[i++] else a[j++]
    while (i <= m) temp[k++] = a[i++]
    while (j <= r) temp[k++] = a[j++]
    for (x in temp.indices) a[l + x] = temp[x]
}
// Time: O(n log n)   Space: O(n)   Stable

sections.heading: Common Mistakes
items: Using subtraction in a comparator, which can overflow (use compareTo or compareBy)
A comparator that is not consistent or transitive, which can crash sort with an exception
Sorting Array<IntArray> by the wrong index or forgetting tie-breakers
Expecting sortedBy to modify the original list (it returns a new list)
Sorting boxed Array<Int> when IntArray would be faster
Assuming primitive array sort is stable (it is not guaranteed; object sorts are)
Using a full sort when only the top K is needed (use a heap or quick select)
Forgetting that sort() on an empty or single-element array is valid and does nothing

sections.heading: Key Takeaways
items: Sorting costs O(n log n) and often simplifies a problem to a scan or greedy pass
Use compareBy and thenBy for multi-key sorting
Never subtract values in a comparator; use compareTo
Object sorts are stable, so you can sort by one key and keep earlier order for ties
Use counting or bucket sort when the value range is small
Use a heap or quick select when you need only the top K or the kth element
